title: The desert mothers
hookLine: Syncletica and others taught that the heart must be tended like a fire

cards: Have you ever tried to light a fire with damp wood? A campfire, a wood stove, a fireplace in an old house. You crouch down and blow, and for a long time you get nothing but smoke.
It stings your eyes. You're sure it's not going to work. Then, if you keep at it, one small flame catches, then another, and suddenly there's warmth.
A woman of the Egyptian desert used that very picture for the life of prayer. Today's word is what people called her: amma.

teach.b: The desert mothers were there too, and people walked out to them just the same as to the abbas. The title was amma, mother, the female twin of abba.
Their sayings sit in the same old collections alongside the men's, fewer of them, but sharp.
One of them is Amma Syncletica of Alexandria.
Tradition says she was a well-off young woman who gave away her inheritance and went to live a life of prayer outside the city, and that younger women gathered around her to learn.

Her saying about fire goes like this, in paraphrase: at the beginning, anyone who draws near to God has a hard struggle, and afterward, a joy that can't be put into words. It's like people lighting a fire.

teach.h: FIRST THE SMOKE, THEN THE FLAME.
teach.b: First the smoke, and tears in their eyes, and then they get what they wanted. So we too have to kindle the divine fire in ourselves, with tears and effort. Notice what she doesn't say.
She doesn't say the smoke means you're doing it wrong. The smoke is part of lighting fires.

She also said something that fits a life of jobs and kids and phones: many who live alone in the mountains behave as if they're in town, and it's possible to live in a crowd and keep solitude in your mind.
Another desert mother, Amma Sarah, is remembered for wrestling with one temptation for thirteen years. She never prayed for it to vanish. She prayed for strength.
That's tending a fire: not a single blaze, but going back again and again, blowing gently on the coals.

how: Many Christians, especially in Orthodox and Catholic monastic communities, read the sayings of the desert mothers alongside the fathers, and some women serve as spiritual mothers who guide others in prayer.

o: a nun who runs a large city convent
mother: a title for a wise desert woman
the wife of a monk living in the desert

games.q: the desert mothers — tap the pairs.

s: only men went to the desert to pray
the desert mothers were there too, and people walked out to them.
Syncletica said smoke means you're doing it wrong
first the smoke and tears, she said, then the fire.
she taught you can keep solitude in a crowd
and that some who live alone behave as if they're in town.

games.q: you're lighting a fire. all you get is smoke, and your eyes are streaming. what does Syncletica's saying suggest?
o: keep going: the smoke comes first.
give up; the wood is bad.
pour water on it and start tomorrow.
games.why: that's her picture of prayer: struggle and tears at first, then a joy that can't be put into words.

practice: Bring to mind one good thing that has gone cold: a habit of prayer, a friendship, a creative project, reading, running, kindness to someone difficult.
Don't try to rebuild the bonfire; just picture blowing gently on the coals, one small breath. If there's smoke, that's normal.

wordCard.voice: Amma. Mother, the twin of abba. The desert's name for its wise women.

orig.note: Greek form of an Aramaic word for mother; the desert's title for a wise woman.

carryVoice: Your line: tend the fire. Smoke comes first, and then the flame. Day two hundred sixty-three.
